list.listitem: Suspect Cushing's Syndrome (CS) in patients with a constellation of symptoms including central obesity, rounded face ("moon facies"), facial plethora, decreased libido, purple striae, menstrual disturbances, hirsutism, erectile dysfunction, hypertension, proximal muscle weakness, posterior neck fat ("buffalo hump"), body bruising, glucose intolerance, osteopenia, and emotional lability or depression. C
The diagnosis of CS begins with a careful history and physical examination and the exclusion of exogenous corticosteroid intake (oral, parental, inhaled, or topical) as an etiology. C

Diagnostic studies for the cause of CS (eg, high-dose dexamethasone suppression test [HD-DST], corticotropin-releasing hormone [CRH] stimulation test, or bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling [BIPSS]) should be performed for patients with suspected CS. C

During the subsequent evaluation of CS, determine whether the hypercortisolism is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) dependent or independent, followed by identification of cortisol suppressibility in ACTH-dependent disease. C
Targeted surgical treatment is recommended for all patients with endogenous CS. A
Second-line treatments include medication, bilateral adrenalectomy, and radiation therapy (for corticotrope tumors). B
Monitor patients periodically for relapse with a 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC), late-night salivary cortisol, or overnight 1-mg DST. C

background.definition: Cushing's Syndrome (CS) is characterized by signs and symptoms resulting from prolonged exposure to elevated levels of free plasma glucocorticoids. Cushing's Disease (CD) is defined as a pituitary driven cause of CS.

list.listitem: The incidence of CS is not well defined, but ranges from 0.2 to 5 per million population per year.
CD is more common in women than men with a female:male ratio of 3-5:1.

The prevalence of CS ranges from 39 to 79 per million in various populations. In some studies, the prevalence is 2% to 5% in patients with hypertension, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, obesity, and early onset osteoporosis.
Subclinical hypercortisolism, biochemical cortisol excess without classic signs or symptoms of CS, is estimated to be 0.2% to 2% of the adult population.
Severe hypercortisolemia induces immunosuppression, which may place patients with untreated CD at higher risk for COVID-19 infection.
Glucocorticoid excess has several causes:
Excessive ACTH secretion from the pituitary gland (CD) 68%.

Ectopic ACTH secretion by various tumors 12% (includes: small cell lung cancer, neuroendocrine:bronchial-thymic-pancreatic carcinoid tumors, medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and gastrinoma).

Adrenal tumors (adenoma 10% or carcinoma 8%). Somatic mutations in PRKACA gene, encoding the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A (PKA), were recently found in about one third of patients with CS caused by adrenocortical adenomas. Other mutations in cyclic AMP signalling including PRKAR1A, GNAS, PDE11A, PDE8B have also been identified.
Adrenal hyperplasia (macronodular 1% or micronodular <1%).
Ectopic CRH syndrome <1%.
Iatrogenic.
Exogenous use of glucocorticoids.
CS can be classified as either ACTH dependent or ACTH independent. ACTH-dependent CS includes CD, ectopic ACTH syndrome (EAS), and rarely ectopic CRH syndrome.53, 54

In CD and ectopic CRH syndrome, the normal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is altered such that the hypercortisolemia does not inhibit the release of ACTH or CRH secretion, respectively. In general, pituitary adenomas function at a higher than normal set point for cortisol feedback inhibition.
In EAS, excessive ACTH of nonpituitary origin leads to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and cortisol oversecretion.
ACTH-independent causes of CS include adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma, adrenal hyperplasia (macronodular and micronodular), and exogenous administration of glucocorticoids.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Medical conditions requiring chronic glucocorticoid therapy: individuals with rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and/or osteoporosis are at increased risk

list.listitem: Suspect CS in patients with a constellation of symptoms including central obesity, rounded face ("moon facies"), facial plethora, deceased libido, purple striae, menstrual disturbances, hirsutism, erectile dysfunction, hypertension, proximal muscle weakness, posterior neck fat ("buffalo hump"), body bruising, glucose intolerance, osteopenia, and emotional lability or depression.1, 53, 54 C
Exclude exogenous corticosteroid intake (oral, parenteral, inhaled, or topical) as an etiology. C
During the evaluation of CS, determine whether the hypercortisolism is ACTH dependent or independent. In ACTH-dependent cases, differentiate suppressible versus nonsuppressible hypercortisolism. C
If initial evaluation for CS is normal with a high clinical suspicion, repeat studies at a later date. C

Use one of four available diagnostic studies (high-dose dexamethasone suppression test [HD-DST], corticotropin-releasing hormone [CRH] stimulation test, imaging studies, or bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling [BIPSS]) to diagnose patients with suspected CS. C
Invasive procedures such as bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling should be the last resort in the evaluation of CS. C
Hypercortisolism can be established by any of the following:
An 11 pm salivary cortisol level above twice the upper limit of normal reference range (>7.0 nmol/L; >0.25 μg/dL).
A 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) value 4-fold greater than the upper limit of normal reference range is rare except in CS and therefore can be considered diagnostic of CS.
An overnight (1 mg) dexamethasone suppression test (DST) with a plasma cortisol level above 1.8 μg/dL (50 nmol/L) may be consistent with CS.

Consider CS in patients exhibiting signs and symptoms of cortisol excess. Central obesity, rounded face ("moon facies"), facial plethora, and decreased libido are seen in the majority of patients (90%-100%).
A multivariate analysis found that the strongest individual predictors of CS are the presence of osteoporosis (aOR 3.6), dorsocervical fat pad (aOR 3.3) and muscular atrophy (aOR 9.0).

Purple striae (wide striae >1 cm), menstrual disturbances, hirsutism, erectile dysfunction, and hypertension are very common (70%-90%), as are proximal muscle weakness, posterior neck fat deposit ("buffalo hump"), body bruising, glucose intolerance, osteopenia, and emotional lability or depression (50%-70%).
Less commonly patients report headache, backache, limb edema, recurrent infections, hypokalemic alkalosis, or nephrolithiasis (20%-50%). Acne and alopecia are uncommon symptoms (0%-20%).

Other features that may suggest CS include changes in mentation, strength or weight not explainable by other conditions; the presence of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (in women: oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea/infertility; in men: decreased libido and impotence); patients with the clinical diagnosis of metabolic syndrome (elevated blood pressure and blood sugar, hyperlipidemia, and increased central body fat); osteoporosis (especially associated with rib fractures) in patients younger than 65 years and those with an incidental adrenal mass.
Clinical studies report a mean delayed time between symptom onset to diagnosis for patients with CS of 34 months (ectopic CS: 14 months; adrenal CS: 30 months; and pituitary CS: 38 months).

Laboratory tests: Initial laboratory testing to document endogenous hypercortisolism can include an 11 pm salivary cortisol, 24-hour UFC (at least two measurements), overnight 1 mg DST, and low-dose (2mg/48 h) DST (see ). Data are conflicting about which test is most accurate.
Laboratory testing to consider in differentiation of CS include HD-DST, CRH stimulation test, and BIPSS (see ).
A morning serum cortisol level <50 nmol/L can be used to exclude CS, unless there is a strong clinical suspicion.

There are no preferred diagnostic studies for the screening or differentiation of CS; however, BIPSS should be used as a last resort for the differentiation of CD versus EAS (see ). The following may help in test interpretation: Suppression of serum cortisol to less than 1.8 μg/dL with a late-night salivary cortisol test has 92% to 100% sensitivity, 93% to 100% specificity, 8.8 positive likelihood ratio (LR) and 0.07 negative LR in differentiating CS from normal individuals. Suppression of serum cortisol to less than 1.8 μg/dL with an overnight 1-mg DST has 95% sensitivity, 80% specificity, 11.6 positive LR and 0.09 negative LR to differentiate CS from normal individuals. A 24-hour urine for UFC excretion is 71% to 100% sensitive, 73% to 100% specific with a 10.6 positive LR and 0.16 negative LR in differentiating CS from normal. The HD-DST (2-day 8 mg testing) has sensitivity of 83%, specificity of 100% in the localization of CS when greater than 90% suppression of UFC and greater than 64% of 17-OH corticosteroid is observed; the positive LR is 7.3 and negative LR 0.18. The CRH stimulation test has a sensitivity and specificity of 91% and 88%, respectively, at a rise of plasma cortisol of 20% above baseline, and a sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 100%, respectively, at a rise of plasma ACTH of 35% above baseline in the localization of CS. BIPSS/CRH is an invasive test that is accurate (94% sensitive and specific) for localization of CS.
A summary of how to proceed with diagnostic studies used in the diagnosis and differentiation of CS can be found in , , and .

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, diagnostic testing may need to be altered to protect patients and providers from infection. The Pituitary Society provides guidance on diagnosis and disease management, making use of virtual visits. For patients with a high likelihood of CS, they recommend limited laboratory evaluation (UFC, ACTH, liver panel, basic metabolic panel), preferably at a smaller local laboratory rather than a Pituitary Center, to reduce viral risk exposure. Imaging may be delayed if preliminary assessment confirms ACTH-dependent CS and no visual symptoms are reported.

Imaging: MRI of the head with and without contrast is the most appropriate neuroendocrine imaging for CS associated with a high ACTH levels to rule out pituitary adenoma. A head CT (with or without contrast) is indicated if MRI is contraindicated.
For cases with suspected thoracic or abdominal tumor causing ectopic ACTH production (see causes), CT, MRI, and nuclear medicine tests are used for localization.
Nuclear medicine imaging using 111In-pentetreotide, 18Fluoro-2-deoxyglucose-positron emission tomography, or 68Gallium-SSTR-PET/CT may be useful in cases of ectopic CS.

For patients with suspected adrenal disease, CT is the primary imaging modality with MRI serving in a complimentary role for indeterminate CT findings or when use of ionizing radiation is undesirable. Ultrasound and fluoroscopy (genitography) are used in children and fetuses to evaluate congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

In a study of 353 patients attending endocrinology units, use of clinical signs of muscular atrophy, osteoporosis, and dorsocervical fat pad and a single late-night salivary cortisol level predicted the presence of CS with an estimated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93. 26 cases of CS were diagnosed based on a low-dose DST. Usefulness of this diagnostic strategy has not been evaluated in primary care.
Exclude exogenous corticosteroid intake (oral, parenteral, inhaled, or topical) as an etiology. C

If CS is clinically suspected, the diagnostic approach can be divided into 2 stages: Stage I: Confirm the presence of hypercortisolism on 3 separate occasions to minimize the possibility of false-positive results (see diagnostic algorithm for CS, ). Stage II: Determine the cause/source of the hypercortisolism (see algorithm for the differentiation of CS, ).

Some patients may not have the complete clinical phenotype of CS and certain clinical diagnoses (ie, metabolic syndrome, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, osteoporosis, and incidental adrenal mass) should prompt a biochemical screening for CS.

Repeat biochemical screening may be necessary to establish episodic or periodic hypercortisolism and to rule out false-positive studies of pseudo-Cushing's states (anxiety, depression, alcoholism, and pregnancy).
Targeted surgical treatment is recommended for all patients with endogenous CS, unless surgery is not possible or is unlikely to significantly reduce glucocorticoid excess. A
Options for persistent or recurrent hypercortisolism after surgery include repeat surgery, radiation therapy, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenalectomy. B

CS requires the evaluation and standard therapy for known complications: hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperlipidemia, coagulopathy, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis, and psychological and cognitive alterations. C

The Endocrine Society (2015) recommends normalizing cortisol levels or action at its receptors to eliminate the signs and symptoms of CS in patients with an established diagnosis of CS and treating comorbidities associated with hypercortisolism.

Ketoconazole (400-1200 mg/day), metyrapone, aminoglutethimide, and etomidate (80 mg/day continuous infusion) are short-term medical options for hypercortisolism. They inhibit adrenal steroidogenesis and may be used preoperatively, if surgical treatment is not possible or has failed, to prevent hypercortisolism.

The Endocrine Society guidelines recommend steroidogenesis inhibitors as second-line treatment after transsphenoidal surgery in patients with CD, either with or without RT/radiosurgery, as primary treatment of ectopic ACTH secretion in patients with occult or metastatic ectopic ACTH secretion, and as adjunctive treatment in adrenocortical carcinoma. They also suggest use of medical therapy to block aberrant hormone receptors for patients with bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia and recommend surgical resection in these cases.
In a case series of 62 patients with CS treated preoperatively with ketoconazole, metyrapone, or both, biochemical control was established in about half with clinical improvement in about one third.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 35 studies of steroidogenesis inhibitors with 1520 patients primarily with CD found pooled percentages of normalization of cortisol ranging from 35.7% for cabergoline to 81.8% for mitotane. Multiple agents were more effective than single agents (65.7% vs. 49.4%, respectively). Severe side effects were reported in 15.2%.

Glucocorticoids are generally prescribed in the perioperative period for transsphenoidal surgery. Steroids should be tapered to physiological doses (hydrocortisone 20 mg in am and 10 mg in pm) when patients are stable. Replacement with glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids is generally required after adrenalectomy.
Pituitary-directed medical treatments in patients with CD is also suggested for those who are not surgical candidates or who have persistent disease after surgery.
Surgical therapy depends on the etiology of CS:

CD: transsphenoidal resection or endoscopic transsphenoidal pituitary surgery remission rates are up to 70% to 90%. Repeat resection may be needed for patients with incomplete resection or a pituitary lesion on imaging. In one population study, early complications of transsphenoidal pituitary surgery were similar for the 960 patients with CD compared to the 12,110 patients without CD with the exception of more urinary/renal complications in the former group.

Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma and adrenal hyperplasia: unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy; the Endocrine Society recommends unilateral resection by an experienced adrenal surgeon for all cases of benign unilateral disease. In a literature review, bilateral adrenalectomy performed for ACTH-dependent CS refractory to other treatment modalities resulted in excellent control of hypercortisolism and resolution of Cushing's-associated signs and symptoms with a median surgical morbidity of 15% and median surgical mortality of 3%. Long-term complications included the development of adrenal crisis and Nelson's syndrome (see follow-up tests).
Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors: localization and resection with node dissection as appropriate.
Following surgical resection for CD, there are 3 possible outcomes: cure, remission with the possibility of the return of hypercortisolism, and persistent hypercortisolism.
Prior to adrenalectomies, a hormonal work-up should be performed to rule out the possibility of an ACTH secreting pheochromocytoma.

The Endocrine Society recommends radiation therapy (RT) when there are concerns about a mass effects or invasion associated with corticotroph adenomas and suggests RT/radiosurgery in patients who have failed transphenoidal surgery or have recurrent CD. Medical therapy should be used to normalize cortisol before administering RT/radiosurgery because this will be needed while awaiting a radiation effect.
Options for persistent or recurrent hypercortisolism after surgery include repeat surgery, radiation therapy, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenalectomy.

CS requires evaluation and standard therapy for its known complications: hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperlipidemia, coagulopathy, metabolic syndrome, and osteoporosis.
CS is also associated with cardiac changes including increased left ventricular mass and subclinical biventricular and left atrial systolic dysfunctions that are reversible after treatment.

In a pilot RCT of 46 women with subclinical CS due to an adrenal incidentaloma and osteoporosis/osteopenia, women randomized to weekly clodronate (a bisphosphonate) plus calcium and vitamin D3 had significant improvement in bone mineral density and reported back pain compared to women on supplements only. After 12 months, no women in the clodronate group and two women in the supplement-only group had new vertebral fractures.
Patients may also report psychological and cognitive problems that require specific management (ie, depression, anxiety, suicidal ideations, mania, and cognitive dysfunction).

In a report of 9 children with CS, successfully treated surgically, who developed significant affective pathology, symptoms included anger-rage outbursts, suicidal ideation, irritability, anxiety, and depression; one child committed suicide.

CS is associated with hypercoagulability with a risk between 1.9% and 2.5% for venous thromboembolism (VTE) not provoked by surgery and 0% to 5.6% postoperatively VTE. Children with CS also have elevated procoagulants, antifibrinolytics, and anticoagulants at baseline compared with controls. The Endocrine Society guidelines suggests evaluation of patients with CS for VTE risk factors and use of perioperative VTE prophylaxis.

In a population study in Denmark, hazard ratios for 343 patients with CS vs. 34,300 controls were: 2.6 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.5-4.7) for VTE, 3.7 (95% CI 2.4-5-5) for myocardial infarction, 2.0 (95% CI 1.3-3.2) for stroke, 1.4 (95% CI 1.0-1.9) for fractures, and 4.9 (95% CI 3.7-6.4) for infection.

When complications of CS are detected, standard medical therapy should be initiated, but with the understanding that the control of these complications may not be reached without resolution of hypercortisolism.
Outcome data for transsphenoidal resection for CD from medical centers with expertise in pituitary surgery showed a remission rate of 70% to 90%.
To determine remission, obtain a 24-hour UFC or overnight 1-mg DST.
Monitor patients periodically for relapse.

Patients not cured by surgical intervention or with malignant disease have a standard mortality ratio (SMR) of about 3.8 compared with controls. This can be contrasted with a SMR of 1.84 (95% CI 1.28-2.65) for all patients with CD and 1.23 (95% CI 0.51-2.97) for patients with initial remission from CD.
Outcome data for transsphenoidal resection for CD from medical centers with expertise in pituitary surgery showed a remission rate of 70% to 90%.
Surgical morbidity and mortality from bilateral adrenalectomy based on 739 patients with CS from 23 studies was 18% and 3%, respectively.
In one case series of 311 patients with CD, the probability of 10-year survival was 95.3%. Most (71.4%) deaths in this population were attributed to cardiovascular causes or infection/sepsis.

Among patients with CS undergoing curative-intended surgery, postsurgical recovery of adrenal function was 82% in ectopic CS, 58% in CD and 38% in adrenal CS in one case series of 230 patients with a mean follow-up of 8 years. The median time to recovery was 0.6 years (interquartile range [IQR], 0.03-1.1 y) in ectopic CS, 1.4 years (IQR, 0.9-3.4 y) in CD, and 2.5 years (IQR, 1.6-5.4 y) in adrenal CS.
In a systematic review of patients with subclinical hypercortisolism undergoing adrenalectomy, the time to achieve eucortisolism was 6.5 months; adrenal insufficiency occurred in 65.3%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 47 articles with 2643 patients, found that although most patients with CD were in remission after treatment and quality of life and cognitive functioning improved, these parameters did not normalize compared to healthy controls.
Higher perioperative levels of ACTH, DHEA, and DHEA-S predicted disease recurrence in one study; recurrence occurred in 11 of 66 patient at a follow-up of 131 months.

The Endocrine Society guidelines recommend care by a multidisciplinary team, including an experienced endocrinologist, who can provide patient education about the disease, treatment options, and what to expect after remission.
Postoperative serum cortisol and 24-hour UFC should be obtained to define cure.

In one study, use of postoperative day 1 cosyntropin stimulation testing was helpful for determining which patients required glucocorticoid replacement following unilateral adrenalectomy for adrenal-dependent hypercortisolism.

Monitor for hypopituitarism after surgery for CD, which includes serum thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, follicle stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, testosterone, insulin-like growth factor-1, growth hormone, prolactin, 8 am cortisol, and ACTH levels. The Endocrine Society guidelines recommend measuring serum sodium several times during the first 5 to 14 days after transsphenoidal surgery, obtaining a free T4 and prolactin within 1 to 2 weeks of surgery, and obtaining a postoperative pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan within 1 to 3 months.

Assess postoperative patients every 3 to 6 months with a serum cortisol or cosyntropin stimulation test after withholding steroids for 24 hours, glucocorticoid replacement can be stopped if cortisol is more than 19 μg/dL (525 nmol/L) for either test. The Endocrine society guidelines recommend measuring late-night salivary or serum cortisol in patients with eucortisolism after transsphenoidal surgery, including patients whose eucortisolism was established by medical treatment before surgery.
The definitive test for cortisol deficiency is the insulin hypoglycemia test.
Continue to monitor patients for relapse (the risk of relapse is ~10%-15%) with a 24-hour UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, or low-dose DST after 24 hours off replacement glucocorticoids.

For patients with at least one intact adrenal gland, obtain follow-up morning cortisol and/or ACTH stimulation tests or insulin-induced hypoglycemia to assess the recovery of the HPA axis; discontinue glucocorticoid treatment when the response to these test(s) is normal.

Monitor patients following bilateral adrenalectomy for the development of Nelson's syndrome (uninhibited growth of pituitary corticotroph adenoma resulting from loss of cortisol feedback inhibition on adenoma growth). The risk for Nelson's syndrome has been reported to be as high as 20% to 35%. The Endocrine Society guidelines recommend regularly evaluating for corticotrope tumor progression using pituitary MRIs and ACTH levels.

For patients with Carney complex, an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by an increased risk of several types of endocrine and non-endocrine tumors, the Endocrine society recommends lifelong follow-up tests for cardiac myxoma and other associated disease (testicular tumors, acromegaly, thyroid lesions).

Adrenalectomized patients should be followed indefinitely with MRI of the pituitary and measurements of basal and dexamethasone-suppressed plasma ACTH. Transsphenoidal surgery or irradiation should be performed before the tumor becomes a macroadenoma.

Following RT, measure serum cortisol or urine free cortisol off-medication at 6- to 12-month intervals to assess its effect or if patients develop new adrenal insufficiency symptoms while on stable medical therapy.
Therapy for persistent or recurrent hypercortisolism is repeat surgery, pituitary radiation therapy, medical therapy, or bilateral adrenal resection.

cell.label: Biochemical confirmation of CS. Order ACTH level.

Two options: (1) High-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Give 8 mg by mouth overnight or 2 mg every 6 h for 48 h; >50% serum cortisol suppression? (2) CRH stimulation test. >20% increase above basal serum cortisol post-CRH or >35% increase above basal serum ACTH post-CRH?

High suspicion for ectopic ACTH syndrome?
Order CT or MRI of adrenals. Suspect primary adrenal disorders: Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, macronodular or micronodular hyperplasia.

feature.caption: Summary of the Diagnostic Studies Used in the Diagnosis and Differentiation of Cushing's Syndrome.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnostic Studies Protocols Interpretation Comments
Late-night salivary cortisol Sample is collected at 23:00 h >0.25 mg/dL is abnormal (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) 1. Simple and convenient
2. Easily repeated
24-h urinary free cortisol Collect urinary cortisol and creatinine for 24 h 4-fold the greater limit of normal can be considered diagnostic for CS 1. If GFR is <30 mL/min, the urinary cortisol measurement may be falsely negative
(High-performance liquid chromatography should be the technique of choice to measure urinary cortisol)
2. Avoid interfering substances such as carbamazepine and digoxin
Low-dose DST A normal response is: Interfering conditions with all DSTs include:
1. Patient collects a baseline 24-h UFC, 17-OHCS, and creatinine beginning at 8 am Plasma cortisol <1.8 μg/dL 1. Decreased dexamethasone absorption
2. Give dexamethasone 0.5 mg orally q6 at 8 am, 2 pm, 8 pm, and 2 am for 8 doses during urine collection Plasma dexamethasone 2.0-6.5 ng/mL 2. Drugs enhancing hepatic dexamethasone metabolism
3. Blood is drawn 2 or 6 h after the last dose for measurement of plasma cortisol, dexamethasone, and ACTH Plasma ACTH <5 pg/mL 3. Increased CBG
4.Urine free cortisol, 17-OHCS, and creatinine excretion is measured on day 2 of dexamethasone administration UFC <10 mg/d on the second day of dexamethasone administration 4. Pseudo-Cushing's states (depression, anxiety, alcoholism, pregnancy)
Urinary 17-OHCS excretion ≤2.5 mg/d 5. Improper urine collection
6. Plasma criteria is more reliable and therefore the preferred criteria for diagnosis
Overnight dexamethasone test 1. One mg dexamethasone orally between 23:00 and 24:00 h Plasma cortisol <1.8 μg/dL
2. Measure fasting plasma cortisol between 08:00 and 09:00 h the following morning Plasma dexamethasone 0.08-6.5 ng/mL
Adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) measurements 1. May be collected at anytime but ideal time is between 23:00 and 24:00 using a 2-site immunoradiometric assay >15 pg/mL suggests ACTH-dependent cause
2. ACTH collection should be in a prechilled EDTA tube, placed in an ice bath, and rapidly delivered to the lab for refrigerated centrifugation <5 pg/mL suggests ACTH-dependent cause
5-15 pg/mL requires further evaluation
HD-DST Serum dexamethasone 8-20 ng/mL in normal patients Interfering conditions include:
1. Patient collects a baseline 24- h UFC, 17-OHS, and creatinine beginning at 8 am, after the 24- h collection 90% suppression of UFC and 64% suppression of 17-OHCS excretion suggests CS 1. Decreased dexamethasone absorption
2. Give dexamethasone 2 mg orally q6 at 8 am, 2 pm, 8 pm,and 2 am for 8 doses while continuing urine collection
2. Drugs enhancing hepatic dexamethasone metabolism
3. Blood is drawn 2 or 6 h after the last dose for measurement of plasma cortisol, dexamethasone, and ACTH
3. Increased CBG
4. Urine cortisol, 17-OHCS, and creatinine excretion is measured at baseline and subsequent days of dexamethasone administration
4. Improper urine collection
Overnight HD-DST 1.8 mg orally between 23:00 and 24:00 h A plasma cortisol suppression above 50% suggests CS
2. Measure 8 am plasma cortisol
CRH stimulation test 1. Basal plasma ACTH and cortisol level Mean increase above baseline ACTH by 35% suggests CS Associated side effects include flushing, and metallic taste in ∼20% of patients
2. Administration of 1 μg/kg or 100 μg of CRH Mean increase above baseline cortisol by 20% suggests CS
3. Sample ACTH at 15 and 30 min and cortisol at 30 and 45 min
CRH-LDDST 1. Starting at noon, dexamethasone (dexa) 0.5 mg orally q6 for a total of 8 doses Cortisol >1.4 μg/dL is abnormal and consistent with CS Helps differentiate mild CS from pseudo-CS
2. CRH (1 μg/kg) is given at 8 am after dexamethasone doses with measurement of cortisol and ACTH q15 min for 1 h
BIPSS/CRH 1. Experienced radiologist catheterizes both IPSs An IPSS to peripheral ACTH ratio (IPS/P) >2.0 in the basal state and /or >3.0 after CRH suggests CS 1. Interfering factor: Anomalous venous drainage may result in a false-negative result
2. ACTH samples are taken at basal and at 3, 5, and 10 minutes after CRH (1 μg/kg or 100 μg iv) simultaneously from both IPS and a peripheral vein
2. Associated with complications of DVT, PE, and brain stem vascular damage
Abbreviations: ACTH, adrenocorticotropic hormone; BIPSS, bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling; CBG, corticotrophin-binding globulin; CRH, corticotropin-releasing hormone; CS, Cushing's syndrome; DST, dexamethasone suppression test; HD-DST, high-dose dexamethasone suppression test; OHCS, hydroxycorticosteroid; UFC, urinary free cortisol.
